title: Mary, again
tomorrow: how can one Church breathe with two lungs?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Lawrence showed the poor as the Church's treasures: the poor first. Today, a wedding about to go wrong.
screen: `THE POOR FIRST.` → `A WEDDING ABOUT TO GO WRONG.`

segments.voice: Parties run out of things: the ice, the food, the patience. At a wedding in Cana, it's the wine, in the middle of the celebration, and the hosts are about to be embarrassed in front of their guests. Mary notices before anyone says it. She goes to her son and says, in the Douay-Rheims Bible, "They have no wine." Then she turns to the servants and says one more thing. It's the answer to a lot more than a party.
screen: `PARTIES RUN OUT OF THINGS.` → `THEY HAVE NO WINE.` → `THEN SHE TURNS TO THE SERVANTS.`

segments.voice: What she says to them is this: "Whatsoever he shall say to you, do ye." Do whatever he tells you. Notice what Mary doesn't do. She doesn't tell Jesus how to fix it. She doesn't wait for a sign from heaven before anyone moves. She names the need honestly, they have no wine, and then she points everyone toward him. The servants do something that looks pointless. They fill stone jars with water, all the way to the brim, and carry some to the steward. It's become wine, the good kind. Here's the one to tell a friend: some readers notice that in John's Gospel, these are the only words Mary speaks. Her whole speaking part is a need named and a finger pointing to her son. Catholics ask Mary to pray for them, and the Church teaches that her role always leads to Christ, never around him. Cana is that in one scene. So when a week feels like the wine has run out, the Cana pattern is short. Say what's missing, plainly. Then do the next thing he's already asked of you, even if it looks like just water.
screen: `SHE NAMES THE NEED.` · `SHE POINTS TO HIM.` · `WATER TO THE BRIM.` · `HER WHOLE SPEAKING PART.` · then, large: `DO WHATEVER HE TELLS YOU.`

segments.voice: Say Mary's line out loud, softly: whatsoever he shall say to you, do ye. Then think of one small thing already asked of you this week, an apology, a kindness, a task you've been putting off, and quietly decide on it. If you pray, you can name your own empty jar to God the way Mary did: plainly, in a few words.
Mary. The mother of Jesus, who at Cana named the need and pointed to her son.
Your line: do whatever he tells you, the next small thing, even if it looks like water. Good night.
